title: WHAT IF THE MOON HIT EARTH?

chapters.name: THE MOON BEGINS TO BREAK APART

lines.text: Tonight, Earth looks peaceful. And yet, the Moon above it looks... wrong. Far too large.
Let's rewind to reality. The Moon sits about 384,400 kilometres away.
And right now, it is not falling towards us. It is drifting away, by about 3.8 centimetres every year.
So for this thought experiment, we need a trigger. Imagine something steals the Moon's orbital momentum.
Everything that follows is a hypothetical simulation, not a prediction.
Slowly, at first, nothing seems to change. Then the Moon begins to fall inwards.
A Moon closer to Earth appears larger in the sky. Today it spans half a degree. Watch that number climb.
Standing on the surface, you would see it swell, night after night, until it dominates the heavens.
The danger is gravity itself. Tidal force falls with the cube of distance.
Halve the distance, and the tides become eight times stronger. Close it to a tenth, and they become a thousand times stronger.
Earth's oceans respond first. Water is pulled into enormous bulges that sweep around the planet.
In this simulation the tides are exaggerated for clarity, but the direction is real: coastlines flood, and then whole plains.
Clouds are dragged into new patterns. Weather, as we know it, ends.
Even the solid ground flexes. Earth's crust would rise and fall by metres, every single day.
Now the Moon itself is in trouble. The near side is pulled harder than the far side, and it begins to stretch.
Cracks race across its surface. Heat from tidal flexing glows through the fractures.
Somewhere near the Roche zone, between about nine and eighteen thousand kilometres, a Moon can come apart.
But note the words 'can' and 'may'. The exact distance depends on the Moon's strength, density, and path. It is an estimate, not a guarantee.
In this branch, the Moon shatters into a river of rubble, and the pieces spread out around Earth.
A vast ring of rock and dust forms, a debris field wider than the planet itself.
Fragments on slightly different orbits drift apart, and collide, and grind each other into dust.
A ring is only one possible outcome. Its fate depends entirely on the orbit of every single fragment.
But in the direct impact branch, the biggest mass of the Moon keeps falling. Its speed: almost ten kilometres every second.
That is about thirty-five thousand kilometres an hour, and it has nothing left to slow it down.
Three... two... one.
The collision releases about three and a half times ten to the thirty joules. Nearly ten million times the asteroid that ended the dinosaurs.
A curtain of molten rock is thrown up through the atmosphere and out into space.
The crust melts. Oceans flash into steam. The sky fills with rock vapour, ash, and fire.
Shock waves race around the world, and the surface is reshaped into a global sea of magma.
Pieces of the Moon, and pieces of Earth, are mixed together in a glowing cloud of debris.
Within hours, nothing of the world we know would remain. Not a coastline, not a mountain, not a trace of life.
So what does this simulation actually tell us? It shows how enormous gravity's reach is, and how fragile a planet is.
And it is not entirely fiction. Our Moon was born from a giant collision, over four billion years ago.
A Mars-sized world struck the young Earth, and from that fire, a Moon was made.
The Moon was born from a collision. So what if, one day, it came back to finish the story?
